title: Should unpaid internships be banned?

turns.speaker: Orla
turns.text: The committee's recommending a straight ban. Any internship over four weeks has to be paid at least the minimum wage.

turns.speaker: Dev
turns.text: I got my entire career from an unpaid one. Three months, no money, and it's the only reason anyone would see me.

turns.speaker: Kim
turns.text: Which is sort of the argument against it, though. You could afford three months without pay. Most people can't.

turns.speaker: Dev
turns.text: I lived with my parents twenty minutes away. Yes, I know.

turns.speaker: Orla
turns.text: That's the whole finding, really. They looked at who takes them, and it's overwhelmingly people whose families are already in the city with a spare room.

turns.speaker: Kim
turns.text: So the profession recruits from the profession, generation after generation, and calls it merit.

turns.speaker: Dev
turns.text: Fine, but what actually happens if you ban them? Do those places create paid roles, or do they just stop offering anything at all?

turns.speaker: Orla
turns.text: Mixed, from the countries that did it. Some cut the numbers. Overall the paid intake went up.

turns.speaker: Dev
turns.text: Up by how much? Because fewer, better positions still means fewer.

turns.speaker: Kim
turns.text: Fewer positions that more people can actually reach, though.

turns.speaker: Kim
turns.text: Ten paid places open to everybody beats forty free ones open to people with a spare room.

turns.speaker: Orla
turns.text: And small charities do get hurt by it. That part of the objection is real and nobody's answered it properly.

turns.speaker: Dev
turns.text: Alright. I think I'm arguing for the ladder I climbed rather than for the ladder.

points: A committee recommends banning unpaid internships longer than four weeks.
Dev credits an unpaid internship for his career, but concedes he could only do it because he lived near his parents.
Orla cites evidence that intakes are dominated by people whose families already live in the city.
Kim argues this makes professions recruit from themselves while calling it merit.
Where bans exist, some employers cut places but paid intake rose overall.
Kim's position is that fewer accessible places beat more inaccessible ones; they agree small charities are genuinely harmed and that objection is unanswered.
